Three Uses of the Law
THREE YOO-siz of thuh LAW
noun phrase (Reformed theology)
The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the moral law of God serves three uses: (1) the civil use (restraining sin in society); (2) the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving the sinner to Christ); (3) the normative use (the rule of grateful obedience for the believer). Articulated by Calvin (Institutes II.7) and the Reformed confessions; the Reformed tradition especially emphasizes the third use.

Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the moral law of God serves three distinct uses in the divine economy. (1) The civil or political use (usus politicus or usus civilis): the law restrains sin and evil in society by the threat of punishment, preserving civil order and curbing the wickedness of even the unregenerate (1 Timothy 1:9-10, the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient). (2) The pedagogical or convicting use (usus paedagogicus or usus elenchticus): the law reveals sin, exposes the sinner's guilt, strips away self-righteousness, and (in the Spirit's work) drives the sinner to despair of self and to flee to Christ (Romans 3:20, by the law is the knowledge of sin; Galatians 3:24, the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ). (3) The normative or didactic use (usus normativus or tertius usus legis, the third use): the law serves as the rule of grateful obedience for the justified believer, guiding him in the path of holiness and revealing the will of God for the Christian life (Psalm 119, the believer's delight in the law; Romans 7:22, I delight in the law of God after the inward man; the moral law written on the heart in the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33). Calvin articulated the three uses in the Institutes (II.7); the Reformed tradition (unlike some Lutheran formulations that emphasize the second use as the principal use) especially emphasizes the third use as the abiding positive role of the law in the believer's sanctification. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive three-uses doctrine, especially the third use against the antinomian denial of the law's abiding positive role.

Webster 1828 Definition

Reformed doctrine that the moral law serves three uses: (1) civil (restraining sin in society); (2) pedagogical (revealing sin, driving to Christ); (3) normative/third use (the rule of grateful obedience for the believer); Calvin Institutes II.7; the Reformed tradition emphasizes the third use.

THREE USES OF THE LAW, n. phr. (Reformed theology) The moral law serves three uses. (1) Civil/political use (usus civilis): restrains sin in society by threat of punishment, preserving civil order (1 Timothy 1:9-10). (2) Pedagogical/convicting use (usus paedagogicus): reveals sin, exposes guilt, drives the sinner to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). (3) Normative/didactic use (tertius usus legis, the third use): the rule of grateful obedience for the justified believer, guiding him in holiness (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22; the law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33). Calvin Institutes II.7. The Reformed tradition especially emphasizes the third use as the law's abiding positive role; held against the antinomian denial.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 1:9-10 — "Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners."

Galatians 3:24 — "Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith."

Romans 7:22 — "For I delight in the law of God after the inward man."

Psalm 119:105 — "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path."

Modern Corruption

The antinomian denial of the third use (the law as the rule of grateful obedience) is the principal contemporary error; the Reformed tradition holds the law's abiding positive role in the believer's sanctification.

expand to see more

The principal contemporary contest over the three uses of the law concerns the third use. The antinomian position (in its various forms, from the historic antinomian controversies to contemporary hyper-grace and easy-believism) denies the third use of the law, treating the law as wholly negative (only restraining the wicked and convicting the sinner, never guiding the believer); the antinomian holds that the believer who is free from the law's condemnation is also free from the law's direction. The Reformed-confessional tradition rejects this: the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience (the third use), written on the heart by the Spirit in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10), delighted in by the regenerate believer (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive three-uses doctrine with particular emphasis on the third use: the believer is freed from the law's condemnation (the law cannot condemn the one who is in Christ, Romans 8:1) but not from the law's direction (the moral law remains the rule of his grateful obedience); the Christian life is the Spirit-empowered obedience to the moral law out of grateful love for the God who saved him, not the antinomian disregard of the law's abiding direction.

Hebrew Roots

Calvin Institutes II.7; three uses: civil (restraining sin), pedagogical (driving to Christ), normative/third use (rule of grateful obedience); Reformed emphasis on the third use.
